# Exact varying-mass moment-centroid paths for interval fibers

Let C be compact and convex in R x R, with positive integer fibers
K_i=[l_i,u_i], widths w_i=u_i-l_i>0, at consecutive integer indices P.
Zero-length fibers may be omitted from every integral below. Fix j in P,
write d_i=i-j, and set M=sum w_i. Define

    T_j=max{sum m_i: 0<=m_i<=w_i, sum d_i m_i=0}.

For 0<t<=T_j let B_j(t) be the interval of continuous centroids of all
dominated sources of mass t and base centroid j. Its ordinary centroid
is denoted c_j(t). A singleton interval has its unique point as centroid.

Throughout this note `A_mu(y)=inf_{H contains y} mu(H)` denotes ABSOLUTE
halfspace depth. Normalized depth is A_mu(y)/M.

This note proves two limited facts about the ACTUAL varying-mass path:

* At t=T_j its centroid is the true centroid of an explicit convex
  subbody. Consequently its original depth is >T_j/3 when that subbody
  has more than one positive fiber, and is at least T_j/2 when the selected
  source has one positive fiber.
  In particular the path contains an OC point if T_j>=3M/4.
* For rational interval endpoints the entire path has an exact finite
  description c_j(t)=A t+B+C/t on rational mass intervals. Its range and
  intersection with a prescribed depth region can therefore be checked
  by finite exact arithmetic, without sampling t.

Neither fact proves that every marginal-center path reaches depth M/4
when T_j<3M/4. No counterexample to that all-mass assertion is claimed.
The archived fixed-half-mass counterexample DOES cross a deep point as
t varies; Section 5 computes its complete path.

## 1. Two strictly concave mass-allocation problems

For fixed retained masses m_i, rearrangement within each uniform interval
gives the largest continuous first moment by taking its upper subinterval
of length m_i, and the smallest by taking its lower subinterval. Therefore

    U(t)=max sum_i (u_i m_i-m_i^2/2),
    V(t)=max sum_i (-l_i m_i-m_i^2/2),                 (1)

where both maximizations have constraints

    0<=m_i<=w_i,  sum m_i=t,  sum d_i m_i=0.

Strict concavity makes each maximizing mass vector unique. The feasible
set of densities is convex, so its moment image fills the whole interval

    B_j(t)=[-V(t)/t,U(t)/t],
    c_j(t)=[U(t)-V(t)]/(2t).                         (2)

All extrema are attained. U and V are concave continuous functions of
t on [0,T_j], with U(0)=V(0)=0. The intervals B_j(t) are decreasing under
inclusion: scale a feasible density at mass t by s/t to keep its centroid
at mass s<t. Convexity of C puts every such centroid in K_j. For t<=w_j,
upper and lower subintervals of K_j alone are feasible; hence

    lim_(t downarrow 0) B_j(t)=K_j,
    lim_(t downarrow 0) c_j(t)=(l_j+u_j)/2.          (3)

This supplies a continuous extension of the path to t=0. Continuity at
positive t follows from (1); in particular its image is one interval.
Merely taking the union of all B_j(t) would recover K_j and is a different,
uninformative selector assertion.

## 2. Exact threshold/coarea identities, with their signs

Write a generic objective in (1) as

    Q_v(t)=max sum_i(v_i m_i-m_i^2/2).

Its finite-dimensional optimality conditions have multipliers b,nu with

    m_i=clamp(v_i-b-nu d_i,0,w_i).                  (4)

These conditions are also sufficient: for any feasible m' the exact
quadratic objective difference is

    grad Q(m) dot (m'-m)-||m'-m||^2/2<=0.

The affine multiplier drops out of the first term, and each remaining
bound residual has the required sign. Necessity follows, for example,
by separating the gradient from the feasible polytope's tangent cone;
this is a finite linear separation, with no regularity assumption on
the active inequalities.

On an open mass interval with fixed free set A={i:0<m_i<w_i} and fixed
full set F, put

    S=|A|, Z=sum_A d_i, ZZ=sum_A d_i^2.

If A has at least two indices, S*ZZ-Z^2>0, and the equations for b,nu are

    S b+Z nu=sum_A v_i+sum_F w_i-t,
    Z b+ZZ nu=sum_A d_i v_i+sum_F d_i w_i.           (5)

Thus masses and multipliers are affine in t, and

    Q_v'(t)=b(t),
    Q_v''(t)=-1/[S-Z^2/ZZ].                        (6)

The denominator is positive. If A consists only of j, the correct
replacement is Q_v''=-1. A single free index i!=j cannot persist while
t varies on an open interval: its base equation fixes its mass. A set
with no free index likewise accounts only for an isolated mass.

For the U source, the actual upper cap is

    x-nu d_i>=b,

so b is its boundary value in fiber j. For the V source, write the
physical lower-cap threshold as b_-(t)=-b_V(t); its cap is
x+nu_-(t)d_i<=b_-(t). Write b_+(t)=b_U(t). Apart from the finitely many
transition masses, (6) gives

    U'=b_+,   (-V)'=b_-,
    c_j(t)=(1/(2t)) integral_0^t [b_+(s)+b_-(s)] ds. (7)

These are the thresholds of TWO separately optimized actual source caps;
they are not assumed equal. The formula is a precise average identity
for the ordinary centroid path, not a claim that the averaged thresholds
are themselves the boundary of one source cap.

To justify the finite transitions and the integration at zero without
a regularity shortcut, fix any of the finitely many empty/free/full
patterns. Equations (5) make its KKT feasibility a finite list of affine
inequalities in t. Its admissible masses form an interval, and its value
is quadratic there. In the sole-free-j case, b is affine; eliminating
the still free nu just compares its finitely many affine upper and lower
bounds, with the same conclusion. The patterns cover every mass except
possibly their endpoints, which continuity supplies. Thus U and V are
continuous piecewise quadratics on finitely many intervals, including
at zero. They are absolutely continuous, and (7) follows. Derivatives
may jump at a transition; no global C^1 assertion is needed.

## 3. Exact finite description and what it decides

If l_i,u_i are rational, T_j, all interval endpoints above, and every
quadratic coefficient are rational. On the common refinement of the
U and V mass intervals, (2) therefore has form

    c_j(t)=A t+B+C/t,                               (8)

with rational A,B,C. On the first interval C=0 by (3). Its extrema on
each closed piece occur at an endpoint or, when admissible, at the
positive root t=sqrt(C/A) of c_j'=0. If A=C=0 the piece is constant.
The full path range is therefore determined by finitely many rational
or quadratic-algebraic numbers, with the t=0 limit recorded separately.

The original depth function on K_j is likewise exactly piecewise affine
for rational interval data. For example, a downward nonvertical cap has
mass

    F(a,y)=sum_i clamp(y+a d_i-l_i,0,w_i).

For fixed y the slope breakpoints are

    a=(l_i-y)/d_i, (u_i-y)/d_i  (i!=j).

Between them F is affine in a, and its finite limits at both infinities
are constant plateaus. Its minimum is attained at a breakpoint or one
of those plateaus. Each resulting function of y is piecewise affine,
with rational breakpoints; the upward mass is M-F(a,y). Vertical closed
caps have constant mass and must also be included (they can also be
checked directly). Thus the all-halfspace depth is the minimum of a
finite set of explicit rational piecewise affine functions.

It follows that a rational absolute depth level has an exactly computable
closed interval of eligible y in K_j. Intersecting it with the path range
decides the all-mass selector for this body, with the qualification that
t=0 is a limit rather than an allowed positive mass. If intersection
occurs only at a path extremum attained solely at t=0, that endpoint
must be excluded. This is a finite method for certifying examples; it is
not a uniform theorem about the sign of that intersection.

## 4. The maximal-capacity endpoint is an actual convex-subbody centroid

The feasible maximizing mass vector at T_j is unique. If the full source
has mean j, it is simply m_i=w_i. Otherwise its structure can be written
explicitly. Suppose the full mean is greater than j. Retain all fibers
i<=j. Among i>j, fill indices in increasing order until their positive
base moment balances the retained negative moment. At most one terminal
index k>j is partial; subsequent fibers are empty. The coefficient test

    1-d_i/d_k >0 for i<k,
    1-d_i/d_k =0 for i=k,
    1-d_i/d_k <0 for i>k                            (9)

is a complete LP optimality certificate: for any feasible allocation,
its mass is the sum of these coefficients times its fiber masses, since
the omitted multiple of the base moment is zero. Every nonzero coefficient
forces the claimed bound to be saturated at a maximizer; the one remaining
mass is forced by base balance. If the crossing is exact, no genuinely
partial fiber remains. The case of full mean less than j is the reflected
suffix construction. If j is an extreme base, only its own fiber can be
retained. This also proves uniqueness in every case.

For this fixed terminal allocation m*, equation (2) gives

    c_j(T_j)= [sum_i m_i*(l_i+u_i)/2]/T_j.          (10)

Now keep every selected full interval. Replace the at most one partial
terminal interval by its CENTERED subinterval of length m_i*, and take
the convex hull of all these retained fibers, denoted C'. Every full
retained fiber is unchanged: it is included and the hull lies in C. The
partial fiber is an endpoint of the new base projection, so its section
is exactly its chosen subinterval. There are no other positive integer
fibers. Consequently the mixed measure of C' is exactly T_j, and its
true centroid is (j,c_j(T_j)), by base balance and (10).

If more than one positive fiber is present, C' is a two-dimensional
convex body. Applying the proved theorem in
`candidate d2cfb29fc2b825cb` gives

    A_mu(j,c_j(T_j)) >= A_(mu restricted C')(j,c_j(T_j))
                         > T_j/3.                 (11)

The first inequality is for absolute masses, for every closed halfspace.
With one positive fiber the subbody centroid has depth exactly T_j/2
in its own source, so original depth is at least T_j/2 instead. Thus,
in particular, T_j>=3M/4 guarantees a positive-mass path point of original
depth at least M/4. This is a sufficient capacity regime, not a lower
bound of 3M/4 on the capacity of every marginal center.

This endpoint identification uses d=1. In higher dimension the centroid
of a partial single-fiber moment body need not be the original fiber
centroid, so neither (10) nor the centered-interval realization has been
asserted there.

## 5. Complete path in the existing five-fiber obstruction

Take the ACTUAL convex interval family from
`candidate b69bd5bdfa7fa03d`:

    K_i=[-w_i,0],  w=(9,75,140,200,25),  j=3,
    M=449,  T_j=250.

The unique marginal median is j=3. The exact KKT pattern enumeration in
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_interval_moment_centroid_path.py` gives the following whole path:

| Mass interval | c_3(t) |
| --- | --- |
| 0<=t<=125/2 | 7t/40-100 |
| 125/2<=t<=100 | (t^2-2000t-12500)/(24t) |
| 100<=t<=235/2 | (-150t-1875)/(2t) |
| 235/2<=t<=385/2 | (-4t^2-860t-77725)/(24t) |
| 385/2<=t<=250 | (5875-200t)/(2t) |

At t=M/2 the value is the previously certified bad center -39025/449.
But at the allowed mass t=235,

    c_3(235)=-175/2,
    A_mu(3,-175/2)=225/2 >449/4.                    (12)

The exact all-cap proof of this last equality is Section 4 of that archived
obstruction, and does not depend on a numerical screen. The present
verifier checks every mass interval by sufficient quadratic KKT conditions
and rational arithmetic, checks their covering and continuity, and checks
both special masses. Hence that fixed-mass counterexample does not extend
to failure of the entire ordinary centroid path.

## Scope

The new positive conclusion is the maximal-capacity endpoint lemma (11),
and the new exact mechanism is the full finite path and threshold-average
description (6)--(8). Neither proves that an arbitrary marginal-center
path intersects the OC depth region in the remaining capacity regime.
No numerical search result is used as evidence for a mathematical claim.
